pedagogy.summary: By upper KS2 children move from 'the heart pumps blood' to the double-loop circulatory system: a four-chambered pump (two atria receive, two ventricles push), one loop to the lungs to pick up oxygen and one loop to the body to deliver it, carried through arteries (away from heart, high pressure), veins (back to heart, valves), and capillaries (walls one cell thick where exchange happens). Blood itself is not a plain red liquid but a mixture — red cells carrying oxygen, white cells fighting infection, platelets for clotting, and plasma. Teach it as a JOURNEY a drop of blood takes, tracing the loop repeatedly until the double circuit and the reason for it (reload oxygen at the lungs, unload it at the body) become obvious. Ground the vessel types in things children can feel and see: the pulse in the wrist/neck is an artery, the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand are veins.
bestPractices: Trace a single drop of blood around the WHOLE double loop, out loud and repeatedly: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (drop O2 low, reload) → left atrium → left ventricle → body → repeat. The double loop only makes sense as a continuous circuit, not a labelled diagram.

Anchor vessel names to the body: find the pulse (an artery pushing), point out surface veins, and explain capillaries as the too-small-to-see meeting point where oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected.

Colour-code by oxygen, not by vessel: blood reddens as it passes the lungs and darkens as the body uses the oxygen — so students see WHY two loops exist, rather than memorising 'arteries red, veins blue' (a misleading shorthand).

Separate the two ideas of 'what blood is made of' from 'where blood goes' — first build the four-part composition (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma) with a jar-of-blood model, then set that mixture moving through the loop.
Use the child's own body as the manipulative: measure resting pulse, then link a faster pump to needing more oxygen delivered — previewing the circulation+breathing integration topic.
keyRepresentations: Double-loop circuit diagram (heart in the middle, lung loop on one side, body loop on the other) traced as a continuous path
Four-chamber cutaway of the heart with arrows showing receive-then-push (atria fill, ventricles pump)
Oxygen colour gradient — blood reddening at the lungs, darkening at the tissues — rather than fixed red/blue vessels
'Jar of blood' separation showing the four components layered (plasma, white cells/platelets, red cells)
The pulse as a felt representation of the heartbeat driving blood through an artery
commonMisconceptions: 'The heart makes blood' — it pumps blood, it does not manufacture it (blood cells are made in bone marrow).
'Blood is just red liquid' — missing that it is a mixture of cells, platelets and plasma, each with a job.
'Arteries are red and veins are blue' — vessels are not coloured; the shorthand refers to oxygen level, and deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue. Veins only look blue through skin.
'Blood does one loop around the body' — missing the double circuit; children often think blood goes heart→body→heart and forget the separate lung trip to reload oxygen.
'The heart is on the left and heart-shaped' — it sits centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, and is a fist-sized muscular pump, not the symbolic shape.
'Capillaries are just tiny tubes' — missing that their one-cell-thick walls are the whole point: they are WHERE exchange happens.

learn.summary: Children aged 9–11 move from 'the heart pumps blood' to the double-loop circulatory system: a four-chambered pump (two atria receive, two ventricles push) driving one loop to the lungs to pick up oxygen and one loop to the body to deliver it, through arteries (away from heart, high pressure), veins (back to heart, with valves) and capillaries (walls one cell thick, where exchange happens). Blood is a mixture — red cells (oxygen), white cells (fight infection), platelets (clotting) and plasma. Teach it as a JOURNEY a drop of blood takes, tracing the circuit repeatedly until the double loop and its purpose become obvious: blood reloads oxygen at the lungs, comes back to the heart to be pumped out again, and unloads oxygen at the body. Ground vessel types in things children can feel: the wrist/neck pulse is an artery; the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand are veins. A driveable flow model is the primary vehicle; anatomy-labelling, a 3D heart for orientation, and a consolidation quiz are complementary scaffolds.

activities.title: Drive the double loop and follow one drop
feedback: If a learner traces only one loop (heart → body → heart), ask: when does the blood go back to the lungs to pick up more oxygen? Then re-run the model inserting the lung trip.
If a learner says the blood is 'used up' at the body, lock the camera on one drop and follow it all the way back to the heart to show the closed circuit.
When the colour change is noticed, prompt: why is going BACK to the lungs necessary — what happens to the blood there?
activities.rationale: Circulation is a dynamic flow process with a driving mechanism; letting the child drive the pump and watch the oxygen colour-gradient recompute is intended to make visible, in a way a static labelled diagram does not animate, why blood must visit the lungs between body trips and how it passes back through the heart in two loops. Colour-coding by oxygen (reddening at the lungs, darkening at the tissues) is intended to target the 'arteries red, veins blue' shorthand directly. This is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Tap or hold a beating-heart control so a drop of blood advances around the whole circuit: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body → repeat.
Watch the blood flush bright red as it passes the lungs and darken as it threads the body's capillaries.
Turn on a 'follow one drop' option that locks the view onto a single cell for its full body → heart → lung → heart → body journey, and say out loud where it reloads and where it unloads oxygen.
Speed up the beat and notice delivery quickens, then link this to why exercise raises heart rate.
Trace the complete loop aloud, repeatedly, so it is experienced as one continuous circuit rather than a labelled diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Blood must pass through the lungs to turn bright red (pick up oxygen) before going round the body again. In humans it then comes back to the heart to be pumped hard out to the body, so the circuit is two loops through the heart: heart → lungs → heart, then heart → body → heart. The same blood keeps circulating; it is never used up.

activities.title: Name the parts in context: heart cutaway and 'jar of blood'
feedback: If a learner says 'the heart makes blood', reframe: the heart is a pump, not a factory — blood cells are made in bone marrow; the heart moves blood.
If a learner calls capillaries 'just tiny tubes', highlight the one-cell-thick wall and ask where oxygen actually leaves the blood.
If a learner thinks blood is 'just red liquid', return to the jar model and ask what each separated layer does.
activities.rationale: This companion reference supports the anatomy-naming and blood-composition curriculum objectives: the curriculum requires naming the main parts and describing blood's components, and this scaffold directly serves that. It is strong for labelling but does not itself show flow or the double-loop logic, so it works best alongside the driveable model rather than as the primary artefact.
sourceClaims: Blood is composed of red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma, each with distinct functions.
Y6 pupils should learn to identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood.
learnerActions: On a four-chamber heart cutaway, tap each chamber and say its job: atria receive (fill), ventricles push (pump).

Tap each vessel type in the flowing context and state its function: artery carries blood away from the heart (feel the pulse as it pushes), vein carries blood back with valves, capillary is the too-small-to-see meeting point where exchange happens — in the body's tissues oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected, while in the lungs it is the other way round.

Explore a 'jar of blood' separation showing the four components in three layers — plasma on top, a thin layer of white cells and platelets together, red cells at the bottom — and match each component to its job (red: carry oxygen; white: fight infection; platelets: clotting; plasma: the liquid that carries everything).
Keep 'what blood is made of' as a separate step from 'where blood goes': build the four-part composition first, then set that mixture moving through the loop.
activities.intendedInsight: The named parts each have a function matched to their structure — capillaries' one-cell-thick walls are the whole point (that is WHERE exchange happens), not merely tiny tubes.

activities.title: Feel your own pump: pulse and the body as manipulative
feedback: If a learner says veins are blue and carry 'dirty' blood, ask whether blood heading TO the lungs is clean or dirty, and which vessel carries it — clarify veins only look blue through skin and deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue.
If a learner draws the symbolic heart shape on the left, point to the breastbone and describe the real fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally and tilted slightly left.
activities.rationale: Anchoring vessel names to sensations the child can feel and see is intended to make the abstract vocabulary concrete, and the pulse-after-exercise link bridges to the circulation+breathing integration topic. This is a proposed anchoring approach, not a validated one.
learnerActions: Find the pulse in your wrist or neck and feel it push — this is an artery.
Point out the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand: these are veins seen through the skin (the blood inside is not blue).
Measure your resting pulse by counting beats over a set time.
Do some brisk activity, measure the pulse again, and explain why a faster pump means more oxygen delivered to the body.
Locate where the heart really sits — centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, about fist-sized — not on the far left and not the symbolic heart shape.
activities.intendedInsight: The pulse is the felt heartbeat driving blood through an artery; when the body needs more oxygen the pump speeds up to deliver it, previewing how circulation and breathing work together.

activities.title: Brief 3D orientation: what shape and where the heart really is
feedback: If a learner expects the symbolic shape, compare it to the 3D muscle and name the difference.
Keep this to orientation only — return to the flat circuit model to reason about the loops, since the double-loop pathway is easiest to trace as a flat continuous circuit.
activities.rationale: A 3D view can usefully convey the heart's real shape and position (a known misconception), but the circulatory logic is a planar circuit; use 3D narrowly for anatomical orientation and not to teach the double loop, where the extra spatial dimension can obscure the path. This is a scoped suggestion, not evidence that 3D adds nothing in general.
learnerActions: Briefly view a 3D heart to see it is a chunky central muscle, not a flat symbolic shape, and to see its real position in the chest.
State in your own words where the heart sits and roughly how big it is.
activities.intendedInsight: The real heart is a fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally behind the breastbone, correcting the symbolic 'heart shape on the left' picture.

activities.title: Consolidate and check: sequence, match, categorise
feedback: Recall-style sequencing and matching confirm vocabulary but do not by themselves show the flow intuition — pair any gaps with a return to the driveable model.
If a learner can list parts but cannot say what is exchanged where, send them back to trace one drop and narrate the pick-up/drop-off on each leg.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, matching and categorising are efficient for consolidating and assessing the naming objective after the model, but they check recall rather than building the flow intuition, so they belong after the driveable experience, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should learn to identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood.
learnerActions: Put the double-loop stages in order: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.
Match each vessel type to its function (artery / vein / capillary).
Categorise the four blood components (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma) by their jobs.
Answer the reasoning prompt: what would go wrong if blood went straight from the body back out to the body again without visiting the lungs first?
activities.intendedInsight: Sequencing, matching and categorising can confirm the named parts are recalled and connected to the reason the lung trip must come before the body trip; but these checks test recall, so they do not by themselves build the flow intuition.

constraints: Curriculum objective (ages 9–11): name the main parts of the circulatory system and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood — including the four chambers, the double loop, and the four blood components.

Colour the blood by oxygen level (reddening at the lungs, darkening at the tissues), NOT fixed 'arteries red, veins blue' — that shorthand is misleading; deoxygenated blood is dark red and veins only look blue through skin.
Keep 'what blood is made of' and 'where blood goes' as two separate build steps.
The labelling/cutaway and 'jar of blood' reference is a scaffold for naming parts; it does not demonstrate flow or the double-loop logic and should accompany, not replace, the flow model.
Use the 3D heart only for brief anatomical orientation (shape and position); it is not the tool for teaching the double loop.
Sequencing/matching/categorising tasks assess and consolidate recall; they do not on their own build the flow intuition, so run them after the model.

A conversation/in-role format is a weaker fit here: there is no central persona or open-ended debate in the mechanism, so an in-role chat may add little over driving and tracing the model — this is a fit judgement, not evidence that dialogue cannot teach.

The driveable model's interaction examples (tap/hold to beat, follow-one-drop camera lock, speed-up control, tap-a-vessel labelling, oxygen colour gradient) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (British Heart Foundation claims on the four-chambered double circulation and on blood composition) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their specifics as unconfirmed pending re-check. Only the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true.

Activities 1, 3 and 4 have sourceClaims set to [] because their rationales concern the proposed medium/anchoring approach, which no source claim directly supports; the retained claims on activities 2 and 5 map to the naming/composition curriculum content those tasks teach, not to any proven efficacy of the interaction.

The original framing that driving the model is 'impossible on a static diagram and unnecessary in 3D' and that 3D 'adds nothing' has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; catalog fit ratings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The capillary-exchange description ('oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected') reflects systemic capillaries; the direction reverses at the lungs. This matches the original's KS2 simplification and is retained as such.

Self-audit: loop order, vessel functions (artery away/high pressure, vein back/valves, capillary one-cell-thick exchange), blood components, and heart position were checked for internal consistency and are coherent as stated; no arithmetic or force/motion claims were present. Grammar in activity 2's artery action ('as it pushing' → 'as it pushes') and the awkward activity 5 intendedInsight were corrected.

The reteachPrerequisiteId references and quiz-step vocabulary from the source have been dropped as internal identifiers; the underlying reteach moves (establish the closed circuit; insert the lung loop; heart-is-a-pump-not-a-factory) are preserved in activity feedback.

probeDeeper: What would go wrong if blood went straight from the body back out to the body again without visiting the lungs first?
People say veins are blue and carry 'dirty' blood. Is the blood going TO your lungs clean or dirty — and which vessel carries it?
Red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma — which of these is doing the oxygen-carrying on these trips?
assess.correctAnswer: Blood makes a double loop. On the trip to the lungs it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen; it returns to the heart, which pumps it out again on the second trip to the body, where it delivers oxygen and nutrients to the cells and collects their carbon-dioxide waste; then it returns to the heart to be sent to the lungs again. Two loops are needed so the blood is re-oxygenated at the lungs before being sent round the body — and the blood keeps returning, it is never used up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood flows out to the body and gets used up — it doesn't come back; it's a one-way path.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the closed circuit: the same blood returns to the heart to be reused; trace a full loop back to the start.
errorPatterns.distractor: The blood flows out to the body and is used up there, so the body makes new blood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes blood ending at the body with no return; may say fresh blood is then made.

errorPatterns.pattern: There is only one loop — heart to body and back — the lungs aren't a separate trip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insert the lung loop: blood must be re-oxygenated at the lungs between body trips; two loops, one heart.
errorPatterns.distractor: It only needs one loop — straight round the body and back to the heart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single body loop and omits the pulmonary (lung) loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart makes or produces the blood.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe the heart as a pump, not a factory; blood is made in the bone marrow — the heart moves it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the heart creates blood rather than pumping it.

responseLevels.gap: Describes a single one-way path or blood being used up and not returning; may say the heart makes blood.
responseLevels.full: Explains the double loop as re-oxygenation at the lungs then delivery to the body, with the blood returning each time, naming what is picked up and dropped off on each leg — and reasons about skipping a loop.
responseLevels.partial: Knows there are two loops and names chambers and vessels, but can't say what is exchanged where — lists parts without explaining why the lung trip must come before the body trip.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Blood leaves your heart, and later the very same blood comes back to your heart again. Why does it need to make TWO different trips — one to your lungs and one to the rest of your body — instead of just one loop around? Explain what the blood picks up or drops off on each trip.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the classic single-loop or 'blood gets used up' model can't justify two trips or say the blood returns. Only a child who understands the double circuit can say what is exchanged at the lungs versus the body. The tier-two 'picks up or drops off on each trip' is precisely where the single-loop model collapses.
